title: AI Game Assets
author: Garkoth
selftext: I been working on a game on unity using AI to help me overcome some problems that im facing, and im up to a point where i wanna lock the art style up, i was looking to buy some assets packs but find what im looking for, i would love to use the 2d ik animations tools on unity so i can change the on the fly for some user customizations but i cant seen to make good art with AI, i tried: chatgpt, gemini, grok, midjourney with gemini giving me the best result until now so i wanna know what should be using?

comments.author: life-v2
comments.body:
[Leonardo.ai](http://Leonardo.ai) is probably your best bet here, it was basically built for game assets and has specific models trained for that exact use case.

Freepik also has a solid library of 2D game asset styles if you need reference or base elements to work from. Might save you a lot of generation attempts.

comments.author: Okklay
comments.body:
It depends on Art style.  
For Anime Visual Novel Style, there are a lot of AI models that do Anime characters.  
For Pixel Art there are a lot of sites and models that do only Pixel Art. Like Retro Diffusion.

comments.author: Embarrassed_Jello123
comments.body: I had a similar issue trying to get consistent AI-generated assets. One thing that helped me was experimenting with tools that generate characters first and then iterating the style from there. I played around with webattle.ai for character concepts and interactions, and it surprisingly helped me refine the style direction before moving to actual asset generation.

comments.author: AliAlHamwi
comments.body:
The Unity 2D IK plan changes what you need from a generator. IK wants the character as separate parts on a transparent sheet, and nearly every AI tool hands you a flat finished sprite instead. So don't ask a model for a rig-ready character. Ask it for a consistent character, and cut it up yourself, once.

The order that works: lock the style first with a few images you actually like. You said Gemini gave you the best stills, so those are your anchor set. Generate every character and every customization item against those anchors, then slice one character into limbs, build the IK rig in Unity by hand, and treat customization as sprite swaps into that same rig. The swaps only line up because the style was enforced at generation time, and style references are the load-bearing feature to shop for. In Ludo.ai, where I work, a reference can carry style without carrying subject, which is exactly what keeps a hat item matching a body it was never drawn with. Scenario has its own version of style lock. Either way the rig stays yours, and that is what makes the on-the-fly customization possible at all.
